title: At the Pharisee's Table: Humility, the Great Banquet, and the Cost
summary: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee's house, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, then teaches the guests to take the lowest seat and the host to invite the poor, who cannot repay. When a guest speaks of the feast in the kingdom of God, Jesus tells of a great banquet whose invited guests make excuses, so the host fills his house with the poor and the outcasts. To the crowds traveling with him he says that discipleship means putting him above family and life itself, and counting the cost.
story: Jesus has just lamented over Jerusalem and spoken of people coming from every direction to recline at table in God's kingdom (13:29). Now he reclines at a real table, and the meal becomes a picture of that coming feast. Who sits where, who gets invited, and who refuses to come are the questions that decide who will share the kingdom's banquet. Then Luke turns from the dinner party to the road, where large crowds are following, and Jesus makes sure they understand where the road leads. The chapter joins the generosity of God's invitation with the seriousness of the response it calls for.
historical:
This is the third meal in a Pharisee's house in Luke (after 7:36 and 11:37), and the third Sabbath healing that provokes objection (after 6:6-11 and 13:10-17). Luke's repeated use of the Pharisees' table as a setting reflects how central meals and purity were to their movement. The parable of the great banquet has a relative in Matthew 22:1-14, where a king gives a wedding feast for his son and the invited guests refuse and even kill his servants; the two versions differ enough that some think Jesus told a similar story on different occasions, while others think both evangelists adapted one parable. The sayings on discipleship have parallels in Matthew 10:37-38, and the salt saying in Matthew 5:13 and Mark 9:50. The rest of the chapter is found only in Luke.

In a later period the command to compel them to come in (verse 23) was put to troubling use. Augustine, in his controversy with the Donatists, a separatist church in North Africa in the early fifth century, cited it in defense of imperial pressure to bring them back into the catholic church, and later writers used it to justify coercion in matters of faith. In context, the servant's task is urgent persuasion of people who would never expect to be invited.
cultural:
Dropsy (edema) was a swelling of the body with retained fluid, often accompanied by great thirst. Greek moralists sometimes used it as a picture of greed, a thirst that drinking only increases, and some interpreters see a link with the grasping for honor that follows.

Meals in the ancient Mediterranean expressed and reinforced status. Seating near the host showed a guest's rank, and the invitation lists of the well-off were exchanges of obligation: you invite me, I invite you, and both of us gain honor. Jesus' instruction to invite those who cannot repay breaks that circle. People with visible disabilities were often excluded from such tables and faced limits on serving as priests (Leviticus 21:17-23). It was customary to send an invitation in advance and then to send a servant when the meal was ready. The excuses are thin: no one buys a field unseen or oxen untested, and while Deuteronomy 24:5 exempted a newly married man from war, it did not excuse him from a banquet he had accepted. To refuse at the last minute was a public insult to the host. Hate in verse 26 reflects a Semitic idiom meaning to love less or to put second, as in Genesis 29:30-31; Matthew 10:37 renders the same thought as loving more than me.
literary: The chapter is set around one meal and moves in four steps: a healing with a question (1-6), advice to guests (7-11), advice to the host (12-14), and a parable prompted by a guest's pious remark (15-24). The parable repeats the list from verse 13 (the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame) in verse 21, tying the host's banquet to the kingdom's. It has three excuses and three sendings of the servant. The final section (25-35) is addressed to the crowds and has two paired parables of counting the cost, a builder and a king, framed by three statements that such a person cannot be my disciple (26, 27, 33). The salt saying closes with a call to hear.

outline.t: A man with dropsy healed on the Sabbath
The parable of the great banquet
The cost of discipleship: tower and war

doctrines.note: The great banquet is God's invitation to his kingdom. It is freely offered and fully prepared; the only way to miss it is to refuse. Those who least expected to be invited end up filling the house.
The kingdom reverses the world's order of honor: the humble are exalted, the self-promoting are humbled, and the poor and disabled are the first to be brought in from the streets.
Discipleship involves a loyalty to Jesus above even family and one's own life. A community formed by this call is marked by humility at table and hospitality to those who cannot pay back.

words.note: Tapeinoo, to humble or bring low. The same word appears in Mary's song, where God lifts up the humble (1:52 uses the related adjective). Verse 11 states a principle that runs through Luke: God himself will humble the proud and exalt the lowly.

Miseo, to hate. In ordinary Greek it means hostility, but in a Semitic idiom it expresses preference, as when Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. Jesus does not command malice toward family but a loyalty to himself so complete that every other love comes second.

Anagkazo, to compel or urge strongly. In the parable it expresses urgent insistence to people who would assume the invitation could not be meant for them, not force. Its later use to justify religious coercion (see the historical note) is a cautionary tale about reading a word out of its story.
Anastasis, resurrection. Jesus points hosts to repayment at the resurrection of the righteous. Generosity that expects no return here is not unrewarded; it is looking toward the age to come.

christ: Jesus is both guest and host in this chapter. At the Pharisee's table he heals, teaches, and exposes the scramble for honor. In the parable the host who throws open his house to the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame is the God whom Jesus reveals, and whose invitation Jesus himself carries through Galilee and toward Jerusalem. He practiced the humility he taught: the one who took the lowest place will be exalted, a pattern Paul sees in Christ, who humbled himself to death on a cross and was exalted (Philippians 2:8-9). And his call to carry a cross and count the cost is spoken by one who has already counted it for himself, on the road to Jerusalem.

hard.q: How can Jesus tell his followers to hate their families?
hard.a: Few sayings sound harsher, and it needs to be read carefully. The word hate is a Semitic idiom for loving less or putting second, as Genesis 29:30-31 uses it of Jacob's two wives, and Matthew's parallel says whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). The same Jesus insists on honoring father and mother (18:20) and condemns those who evade support for their parents (Mark 7:10-13). Still, the idiom should not be softened into nothing. In the first century following Jesus could mean being cast out by family, as it still does for many believers today, and he wants would-be followers to know that loyalty to him may cost the closest relationships. The saying ends with even his own life, which shows that the point is not animosity toward others but the surrender of every competing claim. Many Christians testify that this ordering, far from destroying love for family, purifies it.

questions: Think of a gathering you will host or attend soon. What would it look like to apply Jesus' advice about seats and invitations?
The invited guests had reasonable-sounding excuses: property, work, and marriage. What good things tend to become excuses for you?
Jesus urges would-be followers to count the cost. What has following Jesus cost you, and what might it cost in the future?
